# Kubernetes Microservices Monitoring

A queue-based microservices system on Kubernetes, monitored with Prometheus and Grafana, and horizontally autoscaled under load.

## Architecture

| Service | Role | Port |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Service A** | Job submitter (API) — `POST /submit`, `GET /status/:id` | 3000 |
| **Service B** | Worker — consumes the Redis queue, does CPU-bound work (prime calculation), exposes `/metrics`. Scaled by HPA. | 3001 |
| **Service C** | Stats aggregator — `GET /stats`, `GET /metrics` | 3002 |
| **Redis** | Job queue + result store | 6379 |

Service A pushes jobs onto a Redis list (`job_queue`). Service B (2–10 replicas, autoscaled on CPU) pops jobs, does the work, and writes status/results back to Redis. Service C reads aggregate counters from Redis for `/stats` and exposes them as Prometheus gauges.

## Prerequisites

- Docker Desktop (running)
- [minikube](https://minikube.sigs.k8s.io/) or [Kind](https://kind.sigs.k8s.io/)
- `kubectl`
- [Helm](https://helm.sh/) (for the monitoring stack)
- Node.js 22+ (only needed for local dev outside containers)

---

## Deploy Steps

### On Minikube

**1. Start the cluster**

```powershell
minikube start
```

This project relies on the `ingress` and `metrics-server` addons (needed for the Ingress and the HPA respectively):

```powershell
minikube addons enable ingress
minikube addons enable metrics-server
```

**2. Build the service images and load them into the cluster**

Minikube runs its own container runtime, separate from your host's Docker — images built locally aren't visible to it until loaded explicitly.

```powershell
cd service-a; docker build -t service-a:latest .; cd ..
cd service-b; docker build -t service-b:latest .; cd ..
cd service-c; docker build -t service-c:latest .; cd ..

minikube image load service-a:latest
minikube image load service-b:latest
minikube image load service-c:latest
```

**3. Deploy Redis, the ConfigMap, and the three services**

```powershell
kubectl apply -f k8s/redis.yaml
kubectl apply -f k8s/configmap.yaml
kubectl apply -f k8s/service-a.yaml
kubectl apply -f k8s/service-b.yaml
kubectl apply -f k8s/service-c.yaml
```

Confirm everything is up:

```powershell
kubectl get pods
```

You should see `redis`, `service-a`, `service-b` (x2), and `service-c`, all `Running`.

**4. Install the monitoring stack** (one-time — skip if already installed)

```powershell
helm repo add prometheus-community https://prometheus-community.github.io/helm-charts
helm repo update
helm install prometheus prometheus-community/kube-prometheus-stack -n monitoring --create-namespace
```

Wait for it to come up (a few minutes on first run — it's pulling several images):

```powershell
kubectl get pods -n monitoring
```

**5. Wire up scraping + the custom dashboard**

```powershell
kubectl apply -f k8s/monitoring/service-monitors.yaml
kubectl apply -f k8s/monitoring/dashboards/job-metrics-configmap.yaml
```

**6. Open Grafana**

```powershell
kubectl port-forward -n monitoring svc/prometheus-grafana 3000:80
```

Visit `http://localhost:3000`. Username is `admin`; look up the password with:

```powershell
kubectl get secret --namespace monitoring -l app.kubernetes.io/component=admin-secret -o jsonpath="{.items[0].data.admin-password}" | base64 --decode; echo
```

The custom dashboard is at `http://localhost:3000/d/job-processing-metrics`.
